content: In anatomical terms, the head of an animal refers to the rostral part of the body, which typically contains the brain, eyes, ears, nose, and mouth. These structures are essential for various sensory functions, including vision, hearing, smell, and taste. While some simple organisms lack a head, most bilaterally symmetrical animals possess one. In humans, the skull is divided into two main parts: the cranium, which includes all the skull bones except the mandible, and the mandible, also known as the jawbone. A key feature distinguishing mammals from non-mammals is the presence of three small ear bones, or ossicles, which are the malleus (hammer), incus (anvil), and stapes (stirrup). These ossicles play a critical role in the mammalian sense of hearing. In contrast, other animals typically have a single ear bone called the columella. The cranium itself can be further divided into the skull cap (calvarium) and the base. It is composed of several bones that fuse together at junctions called sutures. Multiple sutures converge to form a region known as the pterion. This fusion process begins in utero to protect the brain, the body’s most vital organ. Although most of the cranial bones fuse before birth, certain areas of fibrous tissue, called fontanelles, remain unfused until puberty. The fontanelle located above the forehead in newborns and young children is particularly easy to identify by touch. The adult cranium consists of several bones, many of which are mirrored on the right and left sides of the skull. These bones are often described using anatomical positional terms to clarify their relationships. For example: The two maxillae are located on either side of the head, inferior and medial to the eye sockets (orbits). The two zygomatic bones are positioned inferior and lateral to the orbits. The two temporal bones cover the area where the ears are located. The single frontal bone lies superior to the orbits. The two parietal bones are posterior to the frontal bone and superior to the temporal bones. The occipital bone is situated at the back of the head. Additional internal bones, which are not easily visible, include the sphenoid bone, ethmoid bone, two lacrimal bones, two nasal bones, two palatine bones, two nasal conchae, and the vomer. In total, there are 14 bones in the human face. The mandible, a separate bone, is attached to the cranium at the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). This joint is crucial for the movement of the mandible, enabling actions such as chewing (mastication), eating, and speaking. When viewed from below, the skull contains several openings, or foramina, the largest of which is the foramen magnum, through which the spinal cord passes. Other foramina allow the passage of arteries, veins, and cranial nerves. When the skull cap is removed, the base of the skull reveals three distinct impressions or fossae. The anterior cranial fossa, the most forward depression, supports the frontal lobe of the brain. The middle cranial fossa, shaped like a butterfly, serves as a base for the temporal lobes of the brain. Its central portion, the sella turcica (Latin for Turkish saddle), houses the pituitary gland, a major endocrine organ. The posterior cranial fossa contains the foramen magnum and accommodates the posterior lobe of the brain and the cerebellum. The human face anatomically extends from the chin to the hairline. The skin of the face is highly pliable and lacks deep fascia, which causes facial wounds to bleed profusely. The face contains five orifices: two for the eyes, two nostrils, and the mouth. Blood supply to the face and much of the scalp is primarily provided by the external carotid artery. Sensory innervation of the face is exclusively supplied by the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V), which branches into three divisions: The ophthalmic division innervates the area above the eyes, including the forehead and most of the nose. The maxillary division innervates the area below the eyes but above the mouth, including the cheeks and part of the nose. The mandibular division innervates the area below the mouth and the sides of the cheeks extending to the ears. However, the mandibular angle (the protrusion on the jawbone) is innervated by the second cervical spinal nerve. The facial muscles include the nasal muscles, zygomatic muscles, muscles of mastication (chewing), and those responsible for facial expression. The occipitofrontalis muscle, which spans the top of the head, consists of two parts: the occipitalis (posterior) and the frontalis (anterior). These two muscles are connected by a fibromuscular tissue called the galea aponeurotica, forming the scalp. This arrangement creates a digastric muscle, which wrinkles the forehead and raises the eyebrows. The frontalis is attached to the skin of the forehead and eyebrows anteriorly and to the superior nuchal line posteriorly. The frontalis is innervated by the temporal nerve, a branch of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), while the occipitalis is innervated by the posterior auricular nerve, another branch of the facial nerve. In non-human animals, the simplest organisms lack a head, but many bilaterally symmetrical species possess one. In vertebrates, the head’s contents are protected by the skull, a bony structure attached to the spine. In many cultures, covering the head is a sign of respect. Head coverings are often required in sacred or religious spaces. Historically, women in Europe, the Middle East, and parts of Asia have covered their hair as a symbol of modesty, though this practice has declined in Europe during the 20th century. However, it remains common in other parts of the world. Certain religious traditions also mandate specific head coverings for men, such as the Jewish skullcap or the Sikh turban, while Muslim women often cover their hair, ears, and neck with a scarf. Headwear can signify status, origin, religious or spiritual beliefs, social grouping, occupation, or fashion preferences. The human head, as the location of the brain, has been a subject of intense study. Early modern research by German physician Franz Joseph Gall led to the pseudoscience of phrenology, which peaked in the 19th century. Phrenology falsely attributed character traits and mental abilities to the shape of the head. At the same time, craniometry, the measurement of the human skull, gained popularity. Unfortunately, such measurements were misused, particularly in Nazi Germany, to support racist pseudoscientific theories. The practice of trepanation, or drilling holes in the skull, has also been advocated for pseudoscientific reasons.
